subsubtopic: INCREASE IN UNEMPLOYMENT-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise to move a motion under the provisions of Standing Order 43. A record 1,303,000 Canadians were out of work in June. This represents a rise of 0.7 per cent from the month previous, and is 10.9 per cent of the work force. For the tenth month in a row there was an increase in the number of jobs lost in the country. In one year 435,000 have disappeared, 121,000 of them last month. Ontario was hardest hit with a loss of 50,000 jobs. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson):
That the Prime Minister, whose disastrous economic policies and continued deficit spending have caused this tragic unemployment situation, immediately call a general election so Canadians, including those out of work, can pass judgment on how he is doing his job and whether he should be allowed to keep it. The only people who deserve to be unemployed in this country are the ones who are running it into the ground.

subsubtopic: MANPOWER MOBILITY ASSISTANCE PROGRAM-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise to move a motion under the provisions of Standing Order 43. Unemployed industrial workers in and around the hard hit West Kootenay community of Salmo, B.C., are angry and cannot understand why taxpayers' dollars have been spent to fill scarce local jobs with applicants from across the country. While the company involved has now agreed to hire local people first, this does not change the fact that such government subsidy of cross-country moving costs, shuffling unemployed Canadians from one jobless area to another, is not only wasteful and unproductive but aggravates already strong feelings of regional resentment and anger. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton):
That the House urge the Minister of Employment and Immigration to review immediately the administration of the Manpower mobility assistance program, instruct his officials at the sending end to consult his officials at the receiving end before the fact of approval, and stop playing musical chairs with the livelihoods and tax dollars of Canadians.

subsubtopic: CALL FOR HOLDING OF GENERAL ELECTION-MOTION UNDER
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, since the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) came to power in 1968, Liberal economic policies have been to spend massive amounts of taxpayers' money on questionable programs until they achieve the highest annual debt in the history of the country. At the same time they adopted a socialist, left-wing, centralist mentality which allowed for no flexibility in the Foreign Investment Review Agency, and in general they have reflected an attitude that discouraged foreign investment, coupled with the stubborn fixation of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) with his new energy program which has caused the destruction of the oil industry in Canada, moved 60 per cent of our oil rigs out of our country, terminated the progress of two tar sands plants and therefore negatively affected both the energy industry of western Canada and the manufacturing basin of Ontario and Quebec. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Fennell):
That the Liberal government, which is causing massive unemployment throughout Canada, take a sabbatical by calling a federal election so that members of the Liberal Party can learn from first-hand experience what unemployment is all about.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in view of the very regrettable absence of the Minister of Finance this morning, I direct my question to the Minister of Employment and Immigration. I might say in passing that the Minister of Finance has his priorities mixed up. The unemployment figures this morning are staggering, and he ought to be in the House to listen to questions.
I am sure that the Minister of Employment and Immigration will recall that last January the unemployment rate in this country stood at 8.6 per cent. By April it had climbed to 9 per cent, and by June, last month, it was up to 10.2 per cent. This morning the published figures put the unemployment level in this country at 10.9 per cent.

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN UNEMPLOYMENT-GOVERNMENT POSITION

It is the highest in recorded history. We have an increase of 52 per cent in unemployment in Canada in one year. We have 435,000 jobs lost in one year alone, and 62,000 of them in just the last month.
Clearly the government's programs are not working and it has instilled absolutely no confidence that it can manage the economy. What will the Minister of Employment and Immigration do about this situation?

The figures this morning show that this is an issue which must be addressed by all Canadians, whether business, labour or in government, in a concerted and co-operative way. It is not a time for fractious dispute. It is time for Canadians to pull together to beat the problem and come to grips with it. It is not

the fault or blame of any one group or sector; it is a problem which must be attacked by all Canadians.

GOVERNMENT APPEAL TO BUSINESS AND LABOUR FOR COOPERATION AND CONSENSUS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Manpower and Immigration. It concerns the very important question of co-operation in Canada right now. Two ministers just referred to the need for that. Yesterday the Prime Minister received support from the business community for a wage control policy, which is hardly surprising because it will increase their profitability. We should not be surprised at that.

The government has acknowledged that unemployment will remain at the present level for the rest of the year. The government said there will be no legislation that will effectively control prices. Considering that a moral approach asking for co-operation in Canada requires fairness in all sections of the community, is it surprising that total support has not been forthcoming from all sectors? speakeroldname: Hon. Donald J. Johnston (President of the Treasury Board) moved
subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OF CANADA
speechtext:
that Bill C-124, respecting compensation in the public sector of Canada, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates.
He said: Madam Speaker, it is with great pleasure that I open the debate on Bill C-124, which concerns the establishment of a compensation restraint program in the federal public service.
Canada is in the middle of an acute recession. One quarter of our production capacity remains idle. There has been an alarming drop in commercial investment and profits. The demand for goods has diminished, both on the domestic market and on our foreign markets. One million two hundred and fifty thousand Canadians are unemployed. Industry and
consumers are suffering as a result of high interest rates which are a by-product of inflation. We must improve our poor performance on the production side. Our trade surplus is the only ray of hope in an economic situation that is otherwise somber and disappointing.
More to the point, we run the risk of seriously jeopardizing our long-term competitive position if we are unable to bring our costs under control. Our inflation performance is worse than that of our key trading partners. At present, Canada's consumer price index is increasing at a rate of more than 11 per cent as compared with one year ago. This is four to five percentage points higher than in the United States and about 6 per cent higher than increases in Germany and Japan. Wage settlements in Canada were in excess of 12 per cent in the first quarter of this year. Our wage settlements are, therefore, running about five percentage points higher than those of our major trading partner, the United States.
In its recently released study, which hon. members undoubtedly saw a few days ago, the OECD identified Canada as having the poorest record among the seven largest member countries in moderating its level of wage increases. To date Canadians by and large have failed to align their wage adjustments to the realities of both the Canadian and world economies. Wage rate settlements are so high as to be in fundamental conflict with reducing inflation, bringing down interest rates and creating employment.
If Canada's economic vitality was less dependent upon its ability to sell goods abroad or upon competition with foreign goods here, it would be much less important how our costs compared with those of our trading competitors. We simply cannot expect to compete once the world recession abates unless we align the increases in our costs of production and our rate of inflation with those of other western trading nations.

During the last few weeks before the last budget was brought down, many informed and concerned Canadians in all professions repeatedly asked the federal government to initiate a wage adjustment standard that would be compatible with the country's present economic capacity and its future well-being. All realized that it was imperative for the federal government to accentuate the anti-inflationary impact of its economic policies by taking a more determined stand on wage rates. The federal public sector compensation restraint program alone cannot resolve all the economic problems Canadians are wrestling with today. It should be seen as a serious and striking example that all Canadians, employers and employees, individually and collectively, must follow if they are the least bit concerned with maintaining their competitive position abroad and their standard of living at home.
July 9, 1982

Wage expectations of Canadian workers can no longer exceed national production without increasing both inflation and unemployment. If the vast majority of Canadians do not agree to wage increases below the expectations they seem to have, inflation will not be reduced either substantially or permanently.

In the federal public service the collective bargaining system during its relatively short 15-year history has worked well. Those who have played a part in operating that system deserve to be commended for the responsible way in which they have conducted their affairs. But in the economic times we have been experiencing and are likely to continue to experience for some time, we simply have to do better. The economy can no longer afford wage increases that match the rate of inflation because they ensure the continuation of inflation at that rate or even higher.
I have heard the suggestion from some commentators and union leaders that this bill singles out the public service for harsh treatment. I reject that charge. Across the country in recent months almost every large employer in the private sector has been forced to take action to curtail wage costs. Employees have been laid off at every level up to top management. Pay increases have been deferred, holidays cut, promotions delayed and hours of work extended. These cuts have not been reflected in figures which purport to compare public and private pay levels. Indeed, public employees have been largely exempted from such restraints or adverse changes in their own working conditions. To this extent they represent a privileged community within the country.
What we are saying in our approach to wage restraint is that leadership, like charity, begins at home. We are not asking others to do what we are not prepared to do ourselves. The restraints also apply to Members of Parliament, to senators, to members of the judiciary, to Crown corporations, to the RCMP and to the Armed Forces. Other than for Members of Parliament, ministers and senators, there will be no reduction in wages or salaries being paid as of June 28, 1982.
The program will apply to employees for a duration of two years from their date of entry into the program, which will be determined by the expiry dates of their current compensation plans or the next scheduled wage rate increase in current compensation plans. The maximum permissible increase in wage rates will be 6 per cent in the first year of application and 5 per cent in the second year. These are not unreasonable increases. The advice tendered to the government from innumerable and varied sources ranges from doing nothing, allowing the existing systems to continue to apply, to freezing or to even rolling back wages already being paid. The program's increases at 6 per cent and 5 per cent are very much in keeping with the inclination of Canadians to seek a moderate approach.
Collective agreements and compensation plans will be extended and continue in force in the two-year period during which the program will apply to employees. In consequence, all compensation conditions and many terms and conditions of
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
employment will remain unchanged for the duration of the program.
The bill provides that the Treasury Board may authorize changes to the terms and conditions of compensation plans other than wage rates, but only in cases where a plan has expired and has not been renewed as of last June 28. This provision will allow the terms and conditions of such expired plans to be brought up to current standards; this provision will not allow terms and conditions to be rolled back. Wage rate increases in such plans will be limited to no more than 9 per cent for the one-year period from the expiry date. Tentative agreements signed by the parties and subsequently implemented without any change will be honoured as part of these transitional arrangements. In such cases, entry into the program will be on the day following the termination date of the compensation plan or on the effective date of the second wage rate increase provided for in the agreement or the plan.

To be successful, a compensation restraint program must be administered as simply as possible and applied across the board; it should contain only a minimum of exemptions or exceptions, require no new administrative organization or hardly any, and affect as little as possible compensation management practices and pay relationships. The proposed program meets all these requirements. In fact, rather than establishing a new governmental organization, the administration of the compensation restraint program in the federal public service will be the responsibility of the Treasury Board, supported in the performance of this duty by its secretariat. The uniform wage rate increases provided under the program will help avoid the complications that would arise from the application of progressive rate increases at various income levels. The applicaton of a uniform rate increase to all compensation plans provides that, as far as possible, present pay scales are maintained. It prevents complex problems arising from the compression and transposition of wages and finally, will provide for an orderly resumption of the collective bargaining process at the end of the program. Wage rates at the bottom of the pay scale in the federal public service compare favourably with those in the private sector. However, there are serious inequities, compared with the private sector, starting at the second management level in the public service. In fact, instead of creating injustice, a uniform rate of increase will prevent existing inequities from getting worse.
It is not the intention of the government to use the wage restraint program to alter the normal structure of pay relationships within the public service, a structure that has been developed so assiduously through the collective bargaining process. Any change in that structure is the proper function of the tax system.
Employees who are at less than job rates will continue to receive increments; those who are subject to performance pay

July 9, 1982
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
plans will continue to receive awards based upon the results of performance appraisals. As a result, employees will continue to progress in their wage or salary ranges as they gain experience and improve performance. This is an important point upon which there is already some misunderstanding and I would remind all hon. members that adjustments are possible in accordance with existing compensation plans. These plans, similar to those which operate in other areas of our economy, including the private sector, will not be changed nor should they be by this particular bill.
Some questions have been raised concerning the propriety of the government continuing to approve or negotiate wage increases for its employees in the days and weeks immediately prior to June 28. Let me set the record straight once again. Hon. members will appreciate that in a collective bargaining regime, once a notice to bargain has been given the parties are obliged to bargain in good faith with a view to concluding a collective agreement. Would it have been good faith on the part of the government to refuse to bargain with its employees or to have deliberately stalled negotiations on the strength of the imminent introduction of the proposed legislation? In my view, the answer is a definite and unequivocable no. Increases were negotiated for the groups concerned on the basis of what was fair and equitable relative to the private sector. As far as those employees are concerned, where the government unilaterally determines the terms of employment, for the groups which we heard of in the House, we saw no reason at all to want to treat them in a manner substantially different from those who are subject to collective bargaining. Their salary reviews were carried out according to the normal schedules. Groups such as Justice department lawyers received the same level of salary increase as those lawyers who are members of the bargaining unit and work in other departments and are not excluded. The unionized lawyers negotiated an 11 per cent increase in April of this year. In short, the government was anxious to treat both their unionized and non-unionized lawyers in a fair and consistent manner.
I should point out, however, that the government is asking the senior executives in the public service to make an additional sacrifice in that the recommendations of the select group of business leaders who advise the government on compensation levels for public service executives will not be approved. The advisory group, as members will recall, recommended a 9.5 per cent increase effective April 1, 1982. Instead, the review date has been brought forward to July 1, 1982, and deputy ministers and other senior executives will have their pay scales adjusted by 6 per cent as of that date. In other words, the 1981 salaries of the most senior public servants will have remained in place for 15 months.
One point I wish to emphasize is that all these groups, those determined unilaterally and those determined by the collective bargaining process prior to the implementation of this program, come under the program at 6 per cent and 5 per cent like everyone else in accordance with the terms of this particular provision of the law.
It is a measure of the serious economic problems facing the country that a proposal to restrain the rate of growth in wage and salary increases in the public sector is necessary. It is necessary because the devastation that inflation brings and has brought must be stopped. This can be done only if all of us, all employed Canadians, make a concerted effort, and indeed a sacrifice, to break the spiralling cost increases in which wages play so important a part. The program that the government has introduced requires a modest sacrifice from public service employees in order to provide benefits and greater opportunities to those Canadians who have been especially hard hit by the ravages of inflation.
The phenomenon of inflation and its impact on countries and individuals today throughout the entire industrialized world is there for all to see. No one is immune from it. Much as a particularly virulent virus, it continues to spread with increasing intensity to claim its victims. Canada cannot contract out of the world in which we rank so high as a trading nation. We cannot permit our economic future to be jeopardized by cost and productivity performance which simply prices us out of markets. If this is allowed to happen, our foreign trade surpluses will disappear, our standard of living will drop dramatically and we will be left behind when our trading partners commence the next surge of world economic growth.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OF CANADA
speechtext: It has already happened.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OF CANADA
speechtext:
Inflation is the enemy. It feeds on our human desires to protect ourselves and it grows on our expectations that we, as individuals and groups, can somehow have more than we earn. We cannot.

The mechanisms we have developed in this country to distribute wealth and revenue, establish the relative value of work and define conditions of employment are numerous and complex. They have been extremely helpful and will continue to be, in my view.
Canadians often speak in disparaging terms about federal public servants and are not always capable of understanding or appreciating their work. These public servants, however, are doing their utmost to serve their fellow citizens. Furthermore, relations between the government and its employees and their representatives are good. We must, therefore, go on working together if we want our country to come through this very difficult period, for the greater benefit of all concerned.

Public servants are no more responsible for inflation than any other group of Canadians.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OF CANADA
speechtext: Or any other group of workers.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OF CANADA
speechtext:
But the whole purpose of the program is much more than simply to restrain wage increases. It signals the start of a national crusade-une croisade nationale- against the crippling effects of inflation, high interest rates and unemployment.
July 9, 1982

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OF CANADA
speechtext: Read the history of the Crusades.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OF CANADA
speechtext: If other sectors follow our leadership and we are successful in this crusade, then everyone will gain from the reduction of inflation that will inevitably ensue. We are challenging the people of Canada to adopt our 6 per cent and 5 per cent target. These are targets that are achievable and which will set our economy back on the track to renewed growth and prosperity. That challenge which I have underlined begins with this bill.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to begin the debate by saying that I believe it is essential to the recovery of this country that we increase its productivity, lessen the demands of its citizens and that the responsibility to accomplish this falls on all Canadians. If there is the crisis of which the minister spoke during his speech, I hope that he will recognize today, as we begin what he calls a national crusade, where the responsibility lies for a great deal of it.
I believe that the problem during the last little while in Canada is that somehow governments which provide leadership have forgotten the biblical injunction that in good years one should store up against the bad years. What has happened, as one finds today as one looks over the devastation which has occurred in the country, is that rather than storing up for the bad years, we have unwisely utilized the tremendous resources, promise and potential that Sir Wilfrid Laurier said was Canada's in the twentieth century. One cannot blame Americans for that and one cannot blame Canadians for that. One does not blame old age pensioners or public servants for that. If governments are prepared to accept the credit when programs and policies work well, then they must equally accept the responsibility when it all collapses. What the minister says is right. The whole thing is close to falling apart. It may apply to the minister, but he is right as it applies to the economy.
As we begin this debate, it is well for every one of us to put it in the appropriate context. It does not matter where we sit in the House of Commons. I would like to put it in this context, because what I am about to say to the House is the bottom line, the balance sheet of years and years of neglect, of virtual dereliction of duty by successive ministers of finance, beginning with the great white hope who practises law on Bay Street and ending with the great white loss who sits in the House of Commons as Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) today.
This is the balance sheet of their stewardship as the Government of Canada. Their agency, Statistics Canada, used the words "The economy is in a tailspin". The gross national product, it told us, fell by 2 per cent in the first quarter, the third consecutive quarter of negative growth in Canada and the largest quarterly decline in 28 years in Canada.
Corporations employ people in Canada. Corporate profits in the first quarter of 1982 were only 41 per cent of the level recorded in the same period in 1981. Manufacturing output in the first quarter of 1982 was only 70 per cent of capacity, the
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
lowest level of capacity utilization since records were first kept in 1961. The transportation industry, which has been the arteries, the lifeblood and the heart of the industrialization and development of the country heretofore, is only operating at 51 per cent of capacity. The Conference Board of Canada says that consumer confidence is at the lowest level in 20 years.
In the first five months of 1982 alone, 4,429 business declared bankruptcy in Canada, up 36 per cent from the same period in 1981 and up 55 per cent from the same period in 1980. When did we ever hear of farm bankruptcies before? They are up by 61 per cent from last year's level and up 111 per cent from 1980. Today, there is 10.9 per cent unemployment in Canada. That statistic, 10 per cent, does not mean much any more, but one must consider it in human terms. There are 1,300,000 Canadians who want to work but cannot find work. Therefore, many dreams have been shattered.
It has been the policy of this government to keep interest rates high, to depress the economy and, boy, has it been successful in doing that! Interest rates have started to climb again as the government attempts to support the dollar. The chartered bank rate is now 18.25 per cent. At least, it was on the eve of the budget. That compares to the rate of 16.5 per cent in the Unites States. At the time of the 1980 election when all those promises for success were made, the Canadian chartered bank rate was 14.75 per cent. It was at that time that then finance critic of the then opposition, who is now the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray), said that if it did not go down, he would resign. Well, the bank rates went up, but, unfortunately for Canada, that minister did not go down. Ten years ago the bank rate was 6 per cent. I thought I should say that, because that is the testament of failure. We must remember that this debate is being carried out in the context of the budget of November 12, 1981, which was condemned by the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan), condemned by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin), and condemned by ten colleagues, private members of the Liberal Party, as one of the worst disasters in history, and which was abandoned by the Minister of Finance. That is the situation in which we find ourselves.
In the context of the budget of June 28, 1982 I do not know of any sector of the Canadian economy which has taken the terms and conditions of the budget of 1982 and said: "That will put the wheels on the vehicle for this national crusade." There has been none. When businessmen were in Ottawa yesterday and met with the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), they were there to support the country. I am one of those Members of Parliament who hopes that the consultation with the labour leaders of Canada will be successful. The meeting is probably being held right now, or if it is over, it was held this morning. I say to the minister that I am one of those who hopes that the consultation is successful because I think this country is sick and tired of non-productive confrontation. There is a duty on the government-not just today, it has been there for years-to have this kind of consultation. The minister

July 9, 1982
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
knows full well that that consultation has not taken place. The result of it is that he must begin, as he puts it, a national crusade.
I want the crusade the minister talks about to succeed. However, I tell him there is some doubt in the country about the efficacy, the strength, ability and credibility of some of the crusaders opposite. The Sir Galahad of 1968 in the shining armour on the white charger is now the leader of a decrepit gang and a degenerated government that is devoid of imagination. They have proven it. Sir Galahad's armour is rusting. The horse's head is bowed. It is old and weak. The sword is broken.
I worry about the leadership of this crusade. I have reason to because I sit every day in this House of Commons and I look at the crusaders. One of the problems in Canada is that we suffer from an economic crisis and a crisis in leadership. It is the crisis that has brought us here. For the sake of this country, I hope and pray that that decrepit gang will take some part in sharing with others the opportunity of bringing this country back to the promise that was made about it by a former Liberal Prime Minister who distinguished himself a long time ago.
I say to the government that theirs is a record of destruction. What has happened to Canada is this. This great country of promise has had a government that is not worthy of the country. The country is worth more than the worth of this government. That is apparent wherever one goes.
Yesterday I received calls from a senior executive, a person working in the public service and a retired public servant. As well, I spoke to a housewife in my office. I met a relatively young person, of voting age, on the steps of the House of Commons as I was coming in. The question on the lips of all these people was: "When are you going to get rid of them?" Would that question be asked if there was not the crisis of which I speak? I am convinced that the government is finished. Its mandate has run out. It makes promises but does not deliver. I do not want the potential of this country to run out. I have to say to those people that I regret our system. I have lived in it for ten years. I regret that it requires us to put up with a government of this nature, but that is the system.
I say to the government that there are millions and millions of Canadians asking the same question. They are saying: "Watch out, members of the government, we are millions strong and we won't forget." Some of them are in the public service of Canada. In the minister's speeches in Toronto, Montreal and Vancouver, he made veiled threats about the public service and the fact that they would have to cut back. He spoke as if public servants were some kind of second-class citizens who somehow did not understand the necessity to be, along with other Canadians, part of a national recovery program.
Some of the rhetoric in this country has done a great disservice to the public service of Canada. I have represented public servants for ten years. They are as much concerned about this country and this government as anyone else. They have more reason to know the shortcomings of this government
because they have worked for it for over 14 years. They have seen the promise dissipate.
It is not because there is a problem with the public service that they are being asked to share in what the minister calls the great crusade and what I hope will be a national recovery program. That is not the problem. They are prepared to share in that. Their concern is that they be joined by others in the crusade. Who are those others? There are the members of the House of Commons, the senators and judges who are joined in that crusade by this bill. However, they want to see others join in the crusade. Yesterday a blue ribbon committee met with the Prime Minister. Public servants want to be assured that the members of that committee join them and that they too, in terms of salary increases, endure the same levels. They want to be sure of that.
Public servants want to be assured that there is some responsibility, and I am sure there is, in the labour movement of Canada to share with the public sector. They put some responsibility on the government. They have noted that while their salaries are being fixed by this bill, the goods and services being delivered by federally-controlled monopolies, agencies and boards are not so confined. Those services are only to be monitored. They have heard the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Communications (Mr. Fox) waffle a bit on how tough that monitoring will be. The public servant notices this when he goes to pay his telephone bill, gas bill or for some kind of service which is under federal responsibility. When he notices that kind of thing and he says: "They are treating me just a shade differently than others even within their own jurisdiction", he is going to demand performance on that promise. If that performance does not come through, then he or she is going to wonder down the road what point there was in being on the cutting edge or the leading edge of the national crusade. He is going to ask all of those questions and for answers.
The public service of Canada knows that there is very little difference between living in a house that is overmortgaged and living in a country that is overmortgaged. Canada is mortgaged to the hilt-$20 billion of mortgage, higher per capita than the United States. The public service knows, like everyone else, that it has been the stupidity of the government that has got it there. But he or she is still a citizen of the country. They are going to take part not only in getting the country out of that mess, if that is possible; they are going to take their part, too, in getting that government off the backs of the country. That is something we are looking forward to, Mr. Speaker.
The minister dealt with the bill in some detail. I do not propose to go into that kind of detail. The government is prepared to have the working man and woman in the public service lay their cards on the table. I believe the time has come when everyone had better lay their cards on the table. The public knows what you receive as a salary, Mr. Speaker, as they should; it is a public salary. They know what the ministers
July 9, 1982

receive, they know what Members of Parliament receive, what judges receive. But a strange thing about this government is that its order in council appointments and the salaries that are paid to order in council appointments are kept secret. I think the time has come for us all to lay the cards on the table.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OF CANADA
speechtext:
I believe that part of this bill should be a requirement that those order in council payments, wherever they are made, wherever they come from and whatever job the people concerned do, that are paid out of the public purse of Canada should become public.
If my friend from the New Democratic Party asks a question, I would tell him that if he was in the House from time to time he would read the Order Paper. He would see a bill in my name which, if it were adopted by the government, would do exactly the same thing. But it is time that they came clean, that they disclosed, so that we know who the players are and what the players are paid.
Take, for instance, the post office, that corporation that is supposed to revolutionize delivery in the postal service in Canada. If it does not, the head of that corporation is called to account for it. It may be a measure of his failure, of the people's judgment, to find out how much he is paid. The same thing applies to the new chairman of the CNR. He used to be a member of this House. They all receive a public salary. I do not know how I as a member of the House of Commons or the Canadian public can judge their performance if we do not know what those salaries are.
I have tried honestly to find some justification in my mind and in my heart for the failure to disclose, but all of the reasons that I have had are facile. The big reason is that maybe they would not want to come to work for the public if the public knew. I do not believe that, because 1 asked Michael Warren in a committee one time if he would tell his salary and he said, "Of course I would; I have no personal objection to that, but it is government policy that that not be done." Well, 1 think it is just about time that we reversed that policy.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
Let us lay the cards on the table. The government is asking public servants to lay a portion of their increases on the table; lay the cards on the table.
With respect to other matters, I think there has to be some real political leadership. I was disturbed the other day when 1 found out that some people within the broad public sector have received in this year salary increases of 21 per cent. Here is what they are. I am quoting from a clipping:
As Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau was telling the Commons how the government was leading the way in wage controls, a Tory MP was trying to find why ministerial aides got a 21 per cent raise this year. June 17, Treasury Board President Don Johnston gave the aides a 10 per cent raise-bringing their total raise so far this year to 21 per cent. The budget, brought down June 28, limited civil service raises to 6 per cent this year and 5 per cent next.

Now, leadership is a good thing. Let that leadership begin at the anterooms of the ministers. Get them back to the status quo ante. Roll it back. Be direct, be honest, treat everyone the same, as my friend from Rosedale (Mr. Crombie) says. That is the thesis of the minister's discussion, his little homily today: let us treat everyone the same. It might be a good idea. It might show leadership and it might help bear the pain a little bit that goes with a cutback if that were done. The minister smiles. He knows he should do this, and I hope over the weekend he will reconsider what they have done with respect to these appointments.
There is another matter which I would like the government to consider, in this sense of fairness, as we begin this crusade together. I see the member for Hamilton West (Mr. Hudecki) is sitting in the House. He is an upright man, a physician of good standing. Let him go, as a physician, as a friend, as a colleague, to the minister and ask him to examine what was done, to see if it is not better that there be that change in attitude-that leadership does start at the top, that leadership does start at ministers' offices. It would be helpful. I think it would lead to some credibility with respect to this national program.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I want to tell the minister that all the public service is prepared to go with it, if they see it works, and they are prepared to go with it in the hope that it will work. Some of them said to me that they want to do their part, and I honestly believe that. Let nobody mistake the situation. Controls of any kind are unfair; they break unfairly and they affect people unevenly. Someone called them rough justice, and that is rough justice.
The minister will have received, I know, a letter from the Professional Institute of the Public Service of Canada, dated July 7, 1982, dealing with the agriculture group. They set forth their concern about Bill C-124, but they do talk about the unique circumstances of the negotiation.
I notice, Mr. Speaker, that it is now one o'clock. I would like to take up the matter at this point after the recess.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, without reflection on your colleagues in the chair, let me say I am very pleased you are in the chair for this debate because we share in common many of the problems we are discussing. 1 do not

think it is inappropriate for me to say that because under our system an incumbent of the chair, whether the Speaker or not, is also a member of the House of Commons.
I am sorry the minister is not here. There might be some legitimate reason for his not being here. I am not reflecting on his absence; his parliamentary secretary is here, and I am pleased to note that.
At one o'clock I was expressing some grave concerns- concerns which have been expressed to me-about the unevenness and the bumpiness of any kind of control program. We had an anti-inflation program during the period 1975-76, and at that time there was a great deal of what might be called rough-justice under that program. Well, there is rough justice here, if I can use that phrase. I think 6 per cent and 5 per cent limits have to be a concern to anyone who is interested in equity.
I see the minister is here now. I welcome him back. Depending on one's income in the public service there is a certain roughness involved in the 6 per cent and 5 per cent guidelines.
The interpretations which will be put on some of the provisions of the bill will create problems as well. At one o'clock I was referring to a copy of a letter I received from the Professional Institute of the Public Service of Canada over the signature of its president, Mr. Jack Donegani, dated July 7, 1982 and directed to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston). The letter dealt with the problem of an agricultural group within the public service of Canada comprising some 265 employees.
This is the first example which has come to my attention, Mr. Speaker. I am satisfied that there will be many examples which come to our attention during the next two or three years in which this program is in place, because to some it is by its terms going to apply a lot longer than just two years. As we reach the straggered end of the program, the examples will become even more apparent and it is my prediction that if there is some regret among members of the House that we ever had to venture into this program because of the roughness of its application, the regret will be multiplied towards the end of the program.
In any event, this is what Mr. Donegani wrote to the President of the Treasury Board about this memorandum of agreement for 265 employees:
This memorandum of agreement was signed at approximately 11 a.m. on June 28, 1982-
As an aside, I will call it a date which will live in infamy. It goes on:
-and thereby in accordance with the proposed section 4(2) of Bill C-124 which states in part " ... a compensation plan shall be deemed to be in effect on June 28, 1982 if parties to the plan have, prior to that date, agreed in writing to establish the plan to have effect on the expiration of the previous compensation plan ... ", the Agriculture Group Memorandum of Agreement will not be honoured.
That is the position and the allegation set out in the letter. It continues:
The Agriculture Group collective agreement expiring July 6, 1982 will be extended without change, save for the wage rate increases provided in Section 9 of the Bill.
It goes on, and this is the important paragraph:
The unique circumstances surrounding the negotiations for the Agriculture Group make the application of Section 4(2) most distressing. The parties met on Friday, June 25, and agreed in principle on many issues. The historical, close relationship with the Biological Sciences Group, which was scheduled to bargain on Saturday, June 26, prompted a pause in the Agriculture negotiations. With the settlement of the Biological Sciences Agreement on June 26, the Institute presented a position for settlement of the Agriculture Agreement at the first opportunity-
That happened to be Monday, June 28, budget day. It continues:
The Treasury Board accepted the settlement which now appears in jeopardy.
That seems to be unfair. If the minister went out of his way to say something should apply to lawyers in the Department of Justice, I think it should apply to the people in the Department of Agriculture covered by this agreement. I raise this as an indication of this rough justice which is going to prevail. The minister is going to have to look into this kind of thing, and I hope he will do so.
There was a very sober and serious letter sent to the President of the Treasury Board on July 5, 1982, from Mr. W. J. Robertson, President of the Canadian Air Traffic Controllers Association. They have been much in the news recently. In fact, they have been the subject of a Supreme Court case which I believe has changed the balance in collective bargaining in the public service of Canada quite dramatically, at least for those who think collective bargaining relates only to strikes. It has affected the rights of the government quite dramatically in terms of the provision of services which are important for safety and security, so much so that I now wonder about Clause 6 and Clause 7 of this particular bill, and I am going to deal with them a little later. The writer of the letter pointed to the inequity which can develop in a control situation; said this:
What more pointed dichotomy of the effect of selective controls could be illustrative than one of the examples we face here in Ottawa. The government is allowing oil companies (including PetroCan) in Ontario to sell gasoline in the Ottawa area at six cents per litre more than anywhere else in the province, despite the fact that the only motive of the operators is to reap windfall profits. This one example perfectly illustrates the advantage industry will be able to take of a controlled public service and consumer.
That statement is true and illustrates how important it is that the monitoring of those goods and services to be delivered under the aegis of the federal government must be strict indeed. Nothing will strike at the heart of the good faith- reluctant, angry, but good faith-which will be exhibited, I believe, by the vast majority of public servants to its elements, at least as they affect compensation, than to see those same public servants on the cutting edge of controls, on the cutting edge of the crusade led by the jaded crusaders I talked about earlier, and then find no other crusaders in business, labour, or elsewhere behind them. The government will have to prove that when it said monitoring, it did not mean a wave of the hand at increases. I do not think the case could have been put any more eloquently than it was last night by the hon. member
July 9, 1982

for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans) when he talked about regulated industries and suppliers of goods and services. I hope the government will not forget that.
There is one other area I would like to deal with, Mr. Speaker, in terms of a possible inequity with which the government must cope. It is interesting, is it not, that the government has decided to monitor the production and cost of goods and services over which it has some jurisdiction. It has decided to cap the compensation of its public servants, but when it comes to the professional consultants it hires, there is not a word in the budget. Not a word. I think there is a demonstrated and patent unfairness in that, and I believe the bill is deficient to the degree it does not apply to consultants' fees. With respect to public relations consultants, ministers can make any deal they want, and we know they make deals. When I was in government I used to make deals with consultants.
Since the government is entering into this regime, if it is good for the public service, then it should be good for the consultants and those who work on behalf of the government under contract. What happens in the public service, unfortunately, is that a great deal of the work they could do is contracted out, and there is little opportunity for public servants to test themselves. The regime should apply to contracted professionals such as lawyers, accountants, management and advertising consultants, reporters, architects and others who perform work on behalf of the federal government. It is patently unfair to deal with the public service one way, and deal another way with those people who supplant or work beside the public servants. I think that is an inequity which the government must look into and deal with.

The government has a duty as well to look at all of its programs, those expensive programs which are discretionary. The government has a duty to look at the decentralization program. You have had some interest, I understand, Mr. Speaker, in the decentralization program. Some difference of opinion seems to have developed with respect to the decentralization program. The minister blushes. If I were the architect of such a program I would blush too.
I am looking at a clipping from the Ottawa Citizen for July 8, 1982. It is a story written by Citizen staff writer Peter Maser. I will read part of it because it is most illustrative:
The federal government will not carry through with plans to move 750 jobs in the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources to Sherbrooke, Que. Or will it?
Ottawa MP Lloyd Francis-
I am quoting from the article, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext:
I have always tried to do that, Mr. Speaker, and I want to assure the hon. member for Northumberland-Miramichi (Mr. Dionne) that I will. I am not angry or upset at all with the intervention of the hon. member for Northumberland-Miramichi. 1 think we should be reminded that the occupant of the Chair at all times is deserving of special respect in the House of Commons.
I shall continue now with the article as follows:
Ottawa MP Lloyd Francis took many of his Liberal colleagues by surprise Wednesday by announcing that the $140 million move was dead, a victim of tough economic times and government restraint.
The article then goes on to say that the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Pelletier) did not agree, that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) had said no decision had been taken, and that even a recommendation on the move would not be going to cabinet for another five or six weeks.
At a period of time when we are asking the public service for restraint, I think it is incumbent upon every member of this House of Commons to ask for a review of that kind of program, which is really an excuse for regional development. I think it is incumbent on every member of this House of Commons to ask what is the cost in loss of efficiency, the length of time in the delivery of service and in the operation and administration of the public service of Canada. That is the question I want to put. I am sure that no member of the House, whether an incumbent of the Chair or otherwise, would not agree that at a time of restraint a program like that should be examined. That is what I meant when I said that it is within the context of a restraint bill-and that is the purpose of it- that some programs be looked at. Decentralization is one of them.
We do not have a bucketful of money in Canada. I think it is important the matter was raised and that a definitive statement be made by the President of the Treasury Board. When he asks for restraint and acceptance of restraint by the public service of Canada, he should say: "I have gone to all members of the House who would be potential beneficiaries of these moves in the decentralization program and I have told them that it is necessary, because it is expensive and because we do not have the money, that I ask the same of you and that all of those moves be cancelled".
Perhaps a move like that could be looked at some day in a better time, but cancelled now. 1 think that would add to the element of fairness that the government must have toward its employees and within the government to the private sector, because the thrust of the program that was outlined by the President of the Treasury Board was this: "We are restraining ourselves; we want you to restrain yourselves."

July 9, 1982
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
That is the leadership that has to be shown and I expect an announcement to that effect from the President of the Treasury Board next week. When he comes before the committee with his bill, which I hope will be soon, I hope that he will make that announcement. I will put him on notice now that I will be asking that question because I believe it is important.
I have mentioned the disclosure of salaries, I have mentioned consulting fees and I have mentioned the subject of ministerial staff. I want the President of the Treasury Board to take a look at Bill C-123, the bill on government reorganization. Do you know what is in that bill, Mr. Speaker? One of the provisions in that bill is the appointment of four more parliamentary secretaries. It is interesting that the government has found a way to increase the salaries of some backbenchers of the government party by creating more part-time work. Under this bill parliamentary secretaries are to be appointed to ministers of state who have no portfolio responsibilities. I have to ask my friends in the Liberal Party whether that is the right thing to do in a time of restraint. I hope they will recognize that it is wrong. We ought not to be creating new positions in Parliament if we are asking the public service to join in what has been described as this crusade to national recovery.
If it is right that public servants be part of that crusade- and I think it is-is it not equally right that government backbenchers, the potential parliamentary secretaries who are to be appointed to ministers of state, should say: "We do not need that to be done, Mr. Prime Minister and Mr. President of the Treasury Board. Change Bill C-123. Do not give us that extra perk. Do not put a further drain on the public purse." I think that is the least they could ask.
I want to deal with one matter quickly since the hon. member for Rosedale will also be dealing with it later on today. I am speaking of the effect Bill C-124 will have. In particular I am referring to clauses 6 and 7. I have to confess that, while I approve generally of the matter of restraint, I really question the wisdom and judgment of this part of the bill. Clause 6 provides as follows:
Notwithstanding any other Act of Parliament, but subject to subsection (2), the terms and conditions of every compensation plan that is extended under Section 4 or 5, other than wage rates, shall continue in force without change for the period for which the compensation plan is extended.
Then there is the exception in subclause (2) which I believe the President of the Treasury Board has mentioned. It reads as follows:
The Treasury Board may, where it deems it appropriate, authorize any change to any terms and conditions, other than wage rates, of a compensation plan that would, but for Section 5, have expired before June 28, 1982.
Then Clause 7 provides:
Every collective agreement or arbitral award that includes a compensation plan that is extended under Section 4 or 5 shall, subject to this Part, continue in force without change for the period for which the compensation plan is extended.
I believe that the effect of this clause is to drive a horse and cart through the collective bargaining process in the public service of Canada. Why is that so important? I for one happen to believe that there is more to collective bargaining than the ultimate weapon, the strike. In fact, it was Tommy Douglas, a former premier of Saskatchewan, a former member of the
House and a former leader of the New Democratic Party with vast experience in Parliament over the years, who said that the strike as a weapon was obsolete. If the collective bargaining process means anything at all, it means that there is more to it than just that ultimate weapon.
Why do we collectively bargain? In an enlightened society we collectively bargain so that working conditions can be reasonable, so that there can be understanding through consultation between employers and employees, so that when there are wrongs to be righted they will be pointed out and righted, so that when there are balances to be adjusted they will be adjusted consultatively.
Employer-employee relations in Canada have moved a long way from the coal pits of England. In the 15 years or so of collective bargaining in the public service of Canada there has been a pretty good record. The fact of the matter is that, on whatever basis one wants to measure it, there have been fewer strikes in the public service than anywhere else in Canada. I am told that in 90 years of collective bargaining in the transportation industry there have been only three general strikes, and they were on the railroads. That is a tremendous record of achievement by management, employers and employees. Actually it is a magnificent achievement when we consider the complications, the number of unions and the number of companies. Somehow or other they have used their heads and have managed to settle matters.
The government, for reasons that I cannot comprehend and that the minister did not explain except in terms of restraint, has decided to take a step which must be described as a blunt instrument. I give the President of the Treasury Board and his officials their just due. This bill was prepared in a hurry. It may be that as a result of the speed with which the bill was prepared the question of restraint was approached with a certain sense of crudeness, if I may put it that way, and that upon reflection in time-and there still is some time-they could consider some possible changes to accomplish the restraint they want to accomplish.
I want them to listen carefully to the remarks of the hon. member for Rosedale, but generally speaking I want to ask the President of the Treasury Board a rhetorical question about which he can think over the weekend. Why was it not possible to devise a means by which collective bargaining could carry on and ensure that in terms of compensation, no matter how the parties or the folks would like to distribute it, the compensation would not exceed the limits in the bill? In other words, is this the only way the government could act? Did it have to drive a horse and cart through collective bargaining in order to achieve restraint? Was there not sufficient imagination, foresight and faith in the collective bargaining system that something other than that crude instrument could have been used?

Also I hope it decides that the bargaining process can continue within the bounds of restraint. If the government

I have in my hand a collective agreement, which is just one of hundreds between the Treasury Board and the Professional Institute of the Public Service of Canada and others, but these are deals with nurses. It covers a number of things which are unique to that group. I could spend the afternoon going over them item by item. They are unique in that group and many are non-monetary. There are some people who may think the opposite, but I believe the record has been sound in terms of negotiation.
There is more to negotiation than strike. In fact, many people do not know that public servants can make a choice; they can choose whether to go the conciliation-strike route or the arbitration route. There are many things wrong with arbitration. There is a limitation on things which may be dealt with by arbitration. I have some sympathy when they use the conciliation-strike route because they can bargain more broadly. That is one problem.
There is another deeper problem which is just as significant to negotiating. It concerns a very fundamental industry in the country about which I spoke earlier-the transportation industry. In Canada there are publicly-owned railroads as well as privately owned railroads. The most important are the CNR and the CPR. One is private and one is public. Somehow this vast industry has been able to find the way, through enlightenment and experience, to achieve a certain amount-in fact a remarkable record-of industrial peace, given the complexity of the industry and its size.
The railway unions have divided into four separate bargaining groups. There is the Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers which represents the men who actually operate the trains. There is the United Transportation Union, an amalgamation of former smaller unions representing a range of employees

involved in the operation of trains. These employees include conductors, brakemen and yardmen. The fourth division is the railway employees department, the AFL-CIO of the shop crafts, as they are usually referred to, which is a coalition of skilled trade unions whose members' main function is the maintenance of equipment. There is the Associated NonOperating Railways Unions Non-Ops, which is a coalition of unions representing the largest and most diverse range of railway employees, including office staff, train dispatchers, track maintenance employees, signalmen and more.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) is in the House and he knows how large it is. There are 90,000 employees represented on one side of the bargaining table. It is my understanding that the opposite side is represented by 11 railway companies.

The danger of this is that we will move away from that wider based bargaining to the experience that some of my colleagues have seen in British Columbia. Women fill only 4.3 per cent of senior management positions, but they comprise 82 per cent of the low paid administrative support positions. They are the cleaning ladies, teachers' aides, clerks and office equipment workers who receive salaries from $9,000 to $12,000 a year. It is obviously they who will be hurt by this legislation. The problem is that this program is really not out to fight inflation. In a document leaked to my party leader last year the reason for this program was exposed as follows:
-a program of consultation and public relations aimed at changing public attitudes and expectations would be useful-even though 'the main advantage of the program would be that it would enable the government to be seen doing something about inflation and to lay part of the blame for inflation on the private sector.'
This same document also indicates this:
-"we are not currently facing a wage-driven inflation such as we were in 1975"-instead real wages have fallen for 4 (now 5) consecutive years-
So the government has admitted in its documentation that inflation is not caused by wages. That is a government document I am quoting, not an NDP document, and it admits that the main advantage would be in PR and shifting the blame
away from the government. So how can the government-and in this 1 agree with the spokesman of the official opposition- expect Canadians to believe that members opposite, cabinet ministers and the Prime Minister are the real crusaders? They have not been, Mr. Speaker.
If you check the wage increases of federal civil servants, you will find that they have not kept pace with the cost of living increases in the last five years. In the first quarter of 1978, wage increases in the federal public service were 6.6 per cent. The increase in the consumer price index was 8.8 per cent. In the first quarter of 1970, public service wages increased 6.4 per cent; the CPI went up 9.1 per cent. In 1980, wages increased 6.6 per cent, and the CPI went up 9.4 per cent. In the first quarter of 1981, federal civil service wages increased by 8.8 per cent, and the CPI went up 12.2 per cent. What does this indicate? It indicates that at the present time, even with the right to collective bargaining, federal employees are not keeping up with the cost of living. This bill means that federal civil servants will get only half as much as the increase in the cost of living, assuming that it only increases at the present rate of 12 per cent. If it goes up 15 per cent or 16 per cent, and increases are limited to 6 per cent, then we can see that the federal employees are the real scapegoats of this government program.
We have heard, from some ministers, Mr. Speaker, that somehow this program is going to help the unemployed. Let me point out again that according to the Conference Board study of the AIB, those controls resulted in the loss of several thousands of jobs. I repeat: several thousands of jobs. This program will do the same because Canadians who are having a tough time now making their mortgage payments or paying for their heat will have less money to spend on other goods. In other words, there will be less need for Canadians to produce goods and therefore fewer jobs for Canadians. That is what is happening. You can look at government documentation, at the Conference Board, and you can look at our history and know that is the case, but this government has a very cynical motive and it does not care what happens to Canadian jobs. So we have a program which is both cynical and devious. It will do nothing for the economy but it will meet the stated Liberal objective of "to be seen to be doing something about inflation".
As part of that same government document I referred to earlier, Mr. Speaker, the decision that public servants take the heat is part of a coherent plan which has been laid out and part of which has been already implemented. It is a deliberate plan by this government to take the heat off itself, and just as we have seen a public relations budget, we are seeing a public relations wage control legislation to rescue not the faltering Canadian economy, but simply to rescue the faltering Liberal Party. Surely this government, which can no longer be trusted by Canadians, must resign. Surely this government, which is asking for the co-operation of Canadians, must recognize that it does not have the trust of Canadians. If Canadians are to
July 9, 1982

have any trust in or co-operate with government, they must believe in the integrity of that government, and they do not believe in the integrity of this government.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the House for allowing me to conclude. 1 have almost come to the end of my remarks on this bill. However, 1 would like to say that this bill is going to hurt Canadians and the Canadian economy. It has the potential to make federal employees the scapegoats of federal action. If that is the case, it will poison the relationship between government and its employees for years to come.
Bill C-124 is an unfortunate bill. Not only that, it will not help Canadians overcome the problems they face. This bill will do nothing about inflation. It will do nothing about high interest rates. It will do nothing about the high price of energy. It will do nothing about unemployment.
The bill should be withdrawn. The government should consult with the different sectors of the Canadian economy before introducing a comprehensive package, whatever that might include. But if the government cannot do that, and if it cannot show some economic wisdom rather than political connivance, then the government should resign.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OF CANADA
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 must say I listened with some disappointment to the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy). I think it is appropriate that members of the New Democratic Party stand up and take their traditional roles or make their traditional speeches but when they have finished their ten or fifteen minute introductions, we should hear alternatives from them. We should hear some indication about how this bill might be improved. If they think we should withdraw this bill, we should hear what kind of a bill they would introduce.
The hon. member for Churchill talks pretty glibly about who will be hurt by this legislation. People are not being asked to take a cut; we are asking Canadians, particularly those in the civil service, not to take as large an increase as they had anticipated. There is no cut. I must say that following the opportunity I have had to talk with civil servants, particularly in the Ottawa area, it seems to me they are prepared to make that sacrifice, if that is the appropriate word-but to take that particular cut-

speechtext: You said it is not a cut.

speechtext:
-because they see it as their role and part of their responsibility to the Canadian economy. There are 500,000 civil servants who are in a position to make a significant impact and show some leadership in this field.
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
I compliment the government and the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) for having the courage to bring forward this particular bill as the cutting edge against inflation. As the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) said, the people who will take the leadership are the civil servants at the federal level. They are the ones who will set a pattern, and if they are followed by other segments of the economy at the provincial and municipal level, and certainly in the private sector, we will have a 6 per cent inflation factor in Canada.
The hon. member who preceded me from Churchill spoke very glibly about who will be hurt. I ask him who will be hurt if no action is taken? Will it not be the women in those low paying categories that he was talking about who will suffer? What about the pensioner on a fixed income? They are the people who will be hurt, because if we do not take action of this nature we will very soon we be looking at a 20 per cent inflation factor. Then those people would really have something to complain about because no action was taken by the federal government.
The hon. member says those who will be hurt will be the people earning $9,000 or $11,000 a year. But those people are fortunate to have a job. Today we heard the atrocious unemployment figures. The invidious nature of inflation is that it impacts on the unemployed, particularly, because it is very difficult for them to get back into the job market; even more so if we had an inflation rate of 20 per cent, which I am sure would come to pass if we did not show some leadership at this time.
If the hon. member has a genuine concern for people, and knowing the hon. member personally, I know he has, I do not think he should lose sight of the fact that there are many people unemployed who are looking for some help, guidance and hope. If you listen to the hon. member for Churchill, it would seem that the only light the New Democratic Party sees at the end of the tunnel is that of an oncoming train. That seems to be the kind of hope which the NDP would hold out for our young people and those who are unemployed.
1 am satisfied that this was not an easy decision for the government to take. It was not easy to ask the government's employees, although the government asks itself, members of its party and Members of Parliament, to take a 6 per cent and a 5 per cent increase. The government is saying to its employees, "We are looking to you to help us in this particular fight and in this particular attempt to buoy up the economy and bring down the inflation rate to 6 per cent." I think civil servants, those working out there in the field, the front line troops, are prepared to make that particular move. I think they want to know that when they look around, as the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton said, they will see that they are not alone. I think they want to see employees of provincial governments, the municipal governments and those working in the private sector behind them. If the federal civil servants take this leadership and they are followed, they will feel very good about

the role they have been called upon to play. When the inflation rate comes down to 6 per cent, I hope people will not forget that it was the federal civil servants who led the way to that victory. Certainly I will mention it over and over again in my riding.
The hon. member for Nepean-Carleton mentioned collective bargaining in the civil service. I do not think too many people have to be reminded that it was a Liberal government which gave that particular right to civil servants.
