speechtext:
I have to say that the record has been good. I agree with the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton about that.
I think over all there is something in excess of 200 bargaining units. When you look at the fact that this legislation has been in place over 15 years the record has been excellent. I think the hon. member mentioned one exception, where he thought the settlement was too high. Perhaps it was a caving in, or it might have been more appropriate had the government been a little tougher, but in looking at an excess of 200 collective bargaining units, all operating at different levels with different areas of responsibility, the record has been excellent.
Nobody should kid the civil servants. Nobody should kid people who want to come and work for the federal civil service, that there is free collective bargaining. There is not free collective bargaining. There comes a time when the federal government must take its responsibility and say, "We have to end this strike. We have to pass legislation ordering people back to work because it is inappropriate for the strike to continue beyond a particular time." That is not a problem that the private sector or unions in the private sector face. People in the civil service, whether they are in the federal or the provincial civil service, must face the ultimate reality that when their actions begin to impinge on the Canadian economy and the good of all Canadians then the government or Parliament must take its responsibility. That has been the experience, and I must say to the credit of the unions that it has not been necessary to do it very often.
When the NDP looks at this place of legislation, it has a tendency to forget what has taken place in the past. What about the progressive legislation that has been put in place; not as a result of efforts of the New Democratic Party, though maybe there was some prodding from that party, and not at the initiative of the Progressive Conservative Party, but there was also some prodding from them? The progressive legislation was put in place by consistent and continuing Liberal governments.
If we did not have these in place, what would be the real impact on the unemployed on those who had not made plans for pensions at retirement? This is why we have put in place programs such as unemployment insurance.
Today I received a telephone call from a radio station which was being very critical of the fact that the union in Sudbury
decided to strike, then recognized the dilemma and the difficulties being faced by International Nickel because of current nickel markets, and accepted a settlement that moved the employees from strike pay to unemployment insurance. Thank God for unemployment insurance and that these people have such an opportunity. This not only helps workers who are no longer on strike, who no longer have jobs and face lay-offs until October, because they will be receiving that income, but the whole community of Sudbury-the people selling groceries, the people cutting hair or the people selling clothers. Those moneys are not going into any socks, into deposit certificates or bank accounts; they are going into the economy to the benefit of the workers and certainly to the benefit of the community at large. It was the Liberal government which put that system into place at a time when the economy was in better shape.
I do not need to catalogue all the programs which have been put in place such as an indexed Canada Pension Plan, old age pension, the guaranteed income supplement, the registered retirement savings plan and medicare. All these progressive moves were put in place so that Canadians would be better able to survive in difficult times than those in other countries who do not have the benefit of these particular protections.
1 looked at the percentage at which we were aiming. The 6 per cent figure was not just picked out of the air. After careful study it was determined that when a recovery takes place it would be more devastating than ever if Canadians were not in a position to compete and to participate in the recovery. If they were slowed down in the recovery, then we would really see unemployment and the devastating effects of high inflation. As I said earlier, it would be much higher than the 11.5 per cent or 12 per cent of today.
I understand that some members of the New Democratic Party may be participating in this debate on Monday. Perhaps they will come up with something positive concerning what could be done. The only suggestion I heard so far was that we should increase the size of the deficit and use that money for job creation. If that does not have a stimulative impact upon the economy, then all we would have is a larger deficit.
Also they recommended exchange controls, but when it was pointed out to them that many ordinary Canadians took trips around the world despite present economic conditions in Canada-and I understand it is at record rates even this year-they changed their tune. When hon. members of the NDP recognized that exchange controls would impact upon Canadian travellers going to the United States, abroad or elsewhere, they suggested selective exchange controls and gradually slipped out of their nomenclature. I do not think we will hear very much about exchange controls because every-time they come up with an idea, if it has any practicality, it is adopted and improved upon. God knows, the Liberal Party in the past has not been hesitant to pick up on ideas, to improve upon them and to include them in legislation. But I say to the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) and others, "Please do
July 9, 1982

not bring in exchange controls or selective exchange controls", whatever they might mean in the nomenclature of the New Democratic Party.
Also it was suggested that nothing is being done at the present time. We know that there is tragically high unemployment. We all know that British Columbia's revenue or source of strength for its economy is the sale of timber and lumber and that approximately 90 per cent of its market is in the United States. If Americans are not buying, it is no wonder that the catalogue of small communities mentioned today by a member of the NDP are in difficulty. If they cannot sell their products, the plants close down; of course this causes unemployment. I am not blaming it upon the United States. It is simply an indicator that that is where the markets are and if the Americans are not buying, the Canadian community of 20 to 25 million people is not large enough to absorb the commodity; thus the economy of British Columbia suffers.
Earlier I mentioned the situation faced by International Nickel. Nickel and copper prices are at an all-time low, so this company cannot make a profit. In fact, the market is not out there, to the point where it has to close down shops. I guess it could be producing to some extent to build up massive inventories, but this would be counterproductive in the long run because it may extend the length of the lay-off rather than have any beneficial effect. Thus, a business economic decision has been made in that particular industry.
Getting closer to home, I represent an area which is the petrochemical centre of Canada. The situation last year was that corporations in the United States were saying that they would take X amount of this particular product and that their prospective purchases would be X amount. Then six months later they came back and said that their inventories were too high and that they could not keep up that size of purchase. As a result, a corporation as large as Polysar had to close down for a month. It told its employees to take their holidays and tried to work out some system whereby the impact of the closure was limited as much as possible. It faced the ultimate reality that those purchasers or those markets were telling them that their inventories were too high and that until their economy picks up they would not be of much assistance.
I suppose it is fair ball for the NDP to take a crack at the large salaries which are being paid to the heads of many of these corporations. I had envisioned their salaries to be somewhere around $200,000 or $300,000. Perhaps 1 was thinking back to the 1970 era, but I knew they also had stock options and certainly opportunities as heads of these corporations. The brains, the intelligence and the ability which these people put into these large industries create many of the jobs in Canada. Frankly, the vast majority of Canadian jobs are provided by small business people, but we would ignore at our peril the talent and ability that these giants of industry bring to our economy because they are in positions to know nationally and internationally what is needed to make them successful and competitive. Unless they move around the world to seek out markets and to work hand in glove with the Export Development Corporation and our excellent Minister of State for
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
International Trade (Mr. Lumley), we will be in very difficult economic circumstances because we will not have the advantage of those particular people. It may be fair game to say that they are overpaid, but frankly I do not know how anyone could say so. I should like to know the situations with which their companies are faced, how much money they make and how much the economy benefits from the decisions made by these corporate giants. I have seen them fired when appropriation decisions were not made. I have seen them looking elsewhere because they were unable to produce or to live up to the expectations which were held out for them in the first instance.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. Would the hon. member permit a question?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the poem indicates, I am in high flight right now and I do not want to be shot down in midstream. Perhaps when I complete my remarks I will entertain a question.
I should like to deal with another issue which was raised by the hon. member for Churchill. I was surprised to learn that at least he was reading The Financial Post or the Financial Times. He quoted statistics from one of those two publications. He was being very selective because he did not refer to the increase in salaries from 1970 to 1980 shown in the particular issue from which he quoted. More important, he did not point out the productivity to which reference was made in the article. If we do not get our productivity up, no corporation will be able to succeed, no corporation in Canada will be able to compete in international markets; this is what the article indicated. I commend the hon. member. I am not saying that he should have read it aloud in the House of Commons, but I hope he will have a look at The Financial Post or the Financial Times to see what are the difficulties and what the business community is endeavouring to do. It is the business community, in the final analysis, which provides jobs for the people about whom he and I are both concerned.
There is another group in the community upon which we must depend more and more-the individual entrepreneur. I am proud to say that when I was the former minister of immigration we looked with great favour on the billions-not millions-of dollars that entrepreneurs were bringing into Canada. Immigrants were bringing that money into the country and investing in Canada. They would say to us that this is a great country in which to invest.
Sometimes I wonder, when I hear people being critical of the economy, saying there is no future here, while at the same time I see people moving hundreds of millions of dollars of investment into this country. They do that because they have seen the world and have decided this is the place which provides the greatest opportunity, the place where they want to work, invest and have their children educated. They want their children to have the quality of life which is available in Canada.

July 9, 1982
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
There is not just a small group of people that applies to come to Canada. People can select almost any country in the world, other than their own, in which to live. Anywhere from 800,000 to a million people apply each year to come to Canada. Therefore, when I hear people say there is no hope that their children will never own a home or receive the education which they deserve, and that there will be no jobs for them, I say that is nonsense. The record does not indicate that, and the record in the future will certainly show that this is not the case.
The call for leadership has gone out, and I believe it has been heeded by this government. I believe this particular bill is a step in the right direction. I believe that the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton was correct to point out that when we are dealing with the two bargaining units involving 500 thousand people, there will be some inequities. There is no question about that. If some of these inequities can be corrected, with people still being required to participate in what is sometimes called a "crusade", but what I say is a fight against inflation to bring it down to 6 per cent, I have enough faith and confidence in the President of the Treasury Board that they will be corrected.
The over-all leadership position of the government is clearly correct in this instance. It is never easy to call upon your employees, particularly one half million of them, to take the lead and make the sacrifice. Frankly, I am a little disappointed in what I have heard so far. I hope that the meeting with the labour groups will produce more positive reaction than what I have heard some labour leaders espouse.
1 am less than optimistic about the leader of the Canadian Labour Congress. For the life of me I cannot see this long time Liberal hater and NDP supporter doing anything which will be of any help in this particular instance. For once I would like to see him take a positive stance, not only on behalf of union people but on behalf of the 1.3 million who are now unemployed. If we can get the inflation rate down to 6 per cent, with his co-operation, then his contribution will be phenomenal. He has an opportunity to be a great Canadian, to take a great lead and, at long last, say something tough to the unions.
The union workers are prepared to make the sacrifice, but if they are given a con job by the leaders of the unions, that this is inappropriate and unworkable and that the unions will not participate, I suggest he will be doing a disservice to the union workers, all those who work and the union movement itself.
I recently heard Mr. Samson, the head of the public service union, talking about a war measures act on the economy and a war measures act against civil servants. Hyperbole will not get us anywhere. I ask him to spend some time, not just talking to the leaders or speaking rhetoric to the union leadership but talking to the grassroots members of the civil service. He will discover that they are prepared to make a sacrifice. Admittedly, we must get the message across that others will have to participate in this fight, but if he begins by talking in a negative way, such as Jean Claude Parrot has done, he will be doing a disservice to his union and his country.
I ask union leaders to accept their responsibility. I ask them to cross the lines of management and labour, government and labour confrontation. I ask them in this instance to get on side, for once, with the economy to help lower our inflation rate to 6 per cent.
They should not come out with rhetoric such as that of Dennis McDermott. He said that "if we get 6 per cent instead of 12 per cent we will give them a 6 per cent effort". What kind of garbage is that? What kind of leadership is that? He has access to vast amounts of talent and skill at the Canadian Labour Congress headquarters. He has an obligation to consult with those experts in order to determine how Canada can be helped by the union movement. He had better not let the union movement down at this time because I can honestly tell him that Canadians are just waiting to take a knock at the union members. I do think that is inappropriate because union members have been very responsible and responsive in this country. They have not pursued exorbitant increases in wages. If someone like Dennis McDermott gets them riled up, uses hyperbole and becomes "Dennis the Demagogue", his actions will be a great detriment to Canada, the union movement and, most importantly, to the people who are unemployed at the present time.
As I have said, there will be some inequities in this legislation. Some will suffer and be more disadvantaged than others. That will be the extended role they will be called upon to play. I am old enough to remember one world war. I did not participate in it, but I know that many people in the military went out prepared to do their part, whatever they were called upon to do. There was unfairness at that time as well.
In the First World War, some had to go over the top while others were sitting back in Canada repairing trucks. However, everyone was prepared to do his part and play his role within the limits of his God-given abilities. People were prepared to make the sacrifice and play the role they were asked to play even if it was not fair. War is never fair. There is always someone who is not doing his job or not prepared to take the risk or responsibility. There are those who have to take the responsibility of leadership because others do not want it. That was unfair; some were disadvantaged and suffered as a result. Many gave their lives to that cause.
When Canadians begin to think of unfairness, I ask them to remember that this is the greatest country in the world. This is a country which has and will give them the greatest opportunities. Canadians can be confident that their children will grow up in a free country where they will have benefits never dreamed of. This is truly a land of opportunity, but if we kiss it away now through inaction, not following the lead, we will be shirking our responsibilities.
We cannot allow inflation to rise to somewhere between 30 per cent and 40 per cent and then brag about reducing it. We have an obligation to the Canadian people and the generation of Canadians who made sacrifices in the two wars and the Korean War; we have an obligation to the future generation not to let this opportunity slip away.
July 9, 1982

As Members of Parliament we have an obligation to make recommendations. I have recommended that we should establish a Canada fund. People should be able to have money deducted from their wages to be deposited in this Canada fund. This fund should pay 6 per cent, 7 per cent or 8 per cent of non-taxable interest. This money could be loaned to farmers, and small-business men. I can assure the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) that Canadians would rally around that fund. They would take their money out of their socks and their bank accounts if they knew that they were contributing to the well-being of Canada. This recommendation has not been accepted in its entirety, but it is the germ of an idea which we have an obligation to propose.
As Members of Parliament, we have an obligation to point out to the government and the treasury benches what can be done in our own particular ridings which could help the economy. If this involves asking for a better airport in Sarnia or Calgary, or getting a better port in St. John's, we have that obligation. If we do not perform our functions properly we are doing a disservice to our constituents. While our job entails several responsibilities, our greatest responsibility is not to fail the Canadian public at a time when it is crying for our leadership. The leadership is there. We are prepared to make the move. The civil servant is prepared to make the move. I ask my fellow Canadians not to let the civil servants down, and not to let the country down.
